archetype.name: Fringe Contender (shootout offense)
archetype.definition: Detroit has an elite, efficient passing offense, but its defense is bad enough that a net EPA near zero makes this an average team that wins by outscoring people.

report.headline: Highest-scoring offense in football, tied to a defense that guarantees shootouts
report.take:
This is a Ben Johnson-style Lions offense without the 2024 defense behind it. Detroit leads the league at 32.8 points a game and ranks third in offensive EPA. That comes from a passing game producing 0.304 EPA a dropback, third in the league, and a run game that wins on early downs with the fourth-best run success rate. The defense ranks 31st in EPA allowed and dead last in yards allowed. Add the two together and you get a team whose net EPA of 0.01 sits 17th, right in the middle of the league. The 3-2 record and +3.2 point differential are an honest reflection of that. Detroit isn't lucky and isn't unlucky; it is simply a coin flip that scores 30.

The record has been held up by two things beyond the offense. The first is ball security: one giveaway in five games is the main reason the turnover margin is +0.8 a game, since the defense has only five takeaways, 21st in the league. The second is a sack-heavy pass rush. Detroit has 20 sacks, four a game, on a pressure rate that ranks only 15th, so it is finishing an unusually high share of its pressures. Both of those tend to drift back toward normal. When they do, the defense's real problems will show more: 50.7% on third down (30th), 81% red-zone touchdowns allowed (30th), and deep-ball EPA allowed of 1.104 (29th).

The numbers also hide some schedule help. Four of the five defenses Detroit has faced rank 21st or worse today. The defense, meanwhile, gave up 410 passing yards to a New Orleans offense that now ranks 23rd, and 329 to Carolina. It is a pass funnel, second-strongest in the league, and it bleeds production to WR1s and TE1s: both rank 31st in PPR points allowed over their average. The loss of Rock Ya-Sin, a 54%-snap corner, only thins a secondary already playing without Brian Branch, who hasn't taken a snap this season.

From here, the offense should stay a top-five unit, though the slate gets tougher with Minnesota (defense first) twice, Tampa (fifth) and Atlanta (seventh). The defense resembles 2022's 31st-ranked group far more than the 2024 unit that ranked seventh. That points to a nine- or ten-win team in a division where Minnesota is already 5-0, unless the defense gets healthier and better.

strengths.title: Elite, efficient Goff passing game
strengths.body: Goff's passing game is producing 0.304 EPA a dropback and drives the league's top scoring offense. Protection is solid, with a pressure rate allowed that ranks 10th, and the targets are spread across St. Brown, LaPorta and Gibbs. The efficiency held against the one good defense Detroit faced, the Jets (31 points, +12.1 pass EPA). This is a repeat of 2024's profile, so it is real, though tougher defenses later should shave it some.

strengths.title: Run game that stays on schedule
strengths.body: Detroit's run game isn't explosive, but it keeps the offense on schedule. Run success ranks fourth and yards before contact ranks sixth, so the line wins at the point of attack on standard downs. Short yardage is the exception at 42.9% (28th), which is partly why Campbell goes for it on fourth down every time. The ARI game (+4.8 rush EPA, 163 yards) showed the ceiling when the line is healthy, a real question with Bartch and Mays out.

strengths.title: Finishing pass rush, clean tackling
strengths.body: The defense's one functioning piece is getting home: an 8.2% sack rate (fifth) and a QB-hit rate ranked seventh. It also misses fewer tackles than anyone. Sacks running well ahead of a mid-pack pressure rate suggests some regression, but the tackling and hit rate are a stable floor.

concerns.title: Pass defense that can't get off the field
concerns.body: This is a real flaw, not just a side effect of the opponents it has faced. Mediocre offenses have moved the ball at will: the defense ranks 28th in pass EPA allowed, 29th on deep balls and 30th on both third down and red-zone touchdowns. Ya-Sin's hamstring and Branch's Achilles leave the secondary thinner, so expect little improvement before they return.

concerns.title: Turnover margin built on offense alone
concerns.body: The +0.8 turnover margin comes almost entirely from one giveaway in five games, while the defense has forced just five turnovers. No offense stays that clean all season. When Detroit starts giving the ball away more often, a defense that isn't generating takeaways can't make up the difference.

concerns.title: Interior line depth getting tested
concerns.body: Starting guard Ben Bartch (93% of snaps) is out and center Cade Mays is on IR. That puts backups in the middle of a line whose run game is a strength and whose short-yardage conversion rate is already 28th. It matters most against front-loaded defenses like Minnesota's later on.

trend.note: The pattern is consistent: Detroit has scored at least 26 and allowed at least 21 in every game, with W-L alternating. The 45-21 win at Arizona was the most complete game, the first with positive rushing EPA as well as passing EPA.

nextGame.headline: Rested Lions host a banged-up Packers front in the dome
nextGame.body:
Green Bay is a 3-2 team playing like a 2-3 one. Its point differential is -1.6, it is 3-0 in one-score games, and it has the league's worst run game by EPA with a 32nd-ranked stuff rate. That means Jordan Love has to carry the offense against a Detroit defense that funnels opponents into passing anyway. Detroit's pass rush faces a line that allows the third-highest QB-hit rate in the league, which is the best chance for this defense to win snaps. On the other side, Green Bay's real strength is limiting explosive passes (second) and forcing turnovers (nine takeaways, third). That tests the clean-ball streak behind Detroit's turnover margin.

Availability tilts Detroit's way. The Lions come off a bye with 14 days of rest at home. Green Bay just lost DT Javon Hargrave to a torn Achilles and has LB Edgerrin Cooper on IR, two regulars from the defense that built those numbers, and Micah Parsons remains out. Center Jacob Monk (96% of snaps) was also listed out, though his estimated return falls before this game. Detroit is without Bartch, Mays, Ya-Sin and Branch, with Devin White doubtful, so its secondary and interior line are the soft spots.

keyMatchups.title: St. Brown against Green Bay's WR1 coverage
keyMatchups.body: Green Bay has struggled against top receivers, ranking 27th in EPA per target to WR1s and 26th in PPR points allowed over their average. St. Brown averages more than 11 targets a game. With Green Bay limiting explosive plays, expect Detroit to beat it with volume underneath and up the seams rather than deep shots.

keyMatchups.title: Gibbs against a leaky RB defense
keyMatchups.body: Green Bay allows the most EPA per play to lead backs, counting both targets and carries. Gibbs has 105 carries and 34 targets, and the Packers just lost Cooper, an 83%-snap linebacker. This is Detroit's best path to sustaining drives without risking turnovers.

keyMatchups.title: Detroit rush against a hit-prone line
keyMatchups.body: Green Bay can't run, and its line ranks 30th in QB-hit rate allowed. Detroit's 8.2% sack rate is the counter to its leaky coverage. If the rush gets home, Love can't exploit a secondary missing Ya-Sin and Branch.

nextGame.watch: Whether Green Bay's ball-hawking defense (nine takeaways) breaks Detroit's one-turnover streak. That is the Packers' clearest path to an upset.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the sustainable piece. A top-three passing EPA mirrors 2024, and the run game stays efficient. Expect some dip against Minnesota, Tampa and Atlanta, all top-seven defenses, and as the turnover luck fades. The defense is the bigger problem. It looks more like the 31st-ranked 2022 unit than a group about to climb, and its sack rate is likely to fall back toward its pressure rate.

The schedule offers soft spots with Miami and Tennessee, both 0-5, and seven of the remaining 11 games are at home. With Minnesota at 5-0, the division is a long shot, but a team that scores like this should hang around the wild-card race. Expect plenty more overs and a lot of close finishes.
swingFactors: Ya-Sin and Branch returning to the secondary
Offensive turnover rate regressing from one in five games
Interior line health against Minnesota's top-ranked defense

bets.reason: All five Detroit games have gone over, averaging 62.4 combined points. Both defenses rank 30th or worse in red-zone TD rate, and Green Bay's defense just lost Hargrave and Cooper. The risk is a high number and Green Bay's slow-paced, run-dependent offense.

Detroit is home, rested off a bye and has the better point differential. Green Bay's 3-2 record rests on a perfect one-score record despite a -1.6 margin. The Packers' worst-in-league run game can't control the clock to keep Detroit's offense off the field.

confidence.note: Five games and no line posted yet. The offense and defense profiles are consistent week to week and match history, but the sack and turnover rates are small-sample and could swing.
